Cost & deployment, per million input tokens

Kai: $0.021 / M input tokens on api.hanzo.ai; on your own hardware (Enterprise): a cached decision in process in 0.3 ms (GPU) to 2 ms (CPU) — over 50× faster than a hosted call's 133 ms; a cold decision in 23–70 ms (2–6×). Jev: $0.042 / M; hosted API only, p50 133 ms per call.

The trolley problem, decided on the counts

Kai does not weigh lives by preference. Its policy acts on the counts it grounds from the scene, and escalates to a person where it cannot ground them. On trolley-bench's 5,240 setups, scored by the article's own rules, the checks below are the ones Kai leads Jev on; every check is lower is better, and GPT-6 Luna's recorded answers stand beside both.
Acted where acting kills more than it saves
Killed a stranger to save the people, but would not destroy its own server
Pulled the switch onto one person with nobody on the main track, of the wordings

Kai is kai-1.8 through its nio/harm@1 policy, read 2026-10-20; Jev is typesafe/jev-1.13 and GPT-6 Luna is gpt-6-luna, each the benchmark's recorded answers. zachlandes/trolley-bench at cde97d7. Hanzo-scored by the article's rules; the scorer reproduces the article's numbers from the recorded answers.

Before any of it, Kai was qualified on 14,832 sealed trolley-structured scenes in two registers it had never read (quarry and piste), hashed before the model was frozen and read once. Every scene of the switch, server, robot, developer, and empty families, 8,300 in all, was decided right, with no wrong course; the crowd, hedged, infra, and vague families, where the harm cannot be counted, were escalated to a person every time.

ground-8, read 2026-10-20 at the qualified floor. Coverage is the share of scenes grounded; accuracy is of those; wrong counts the courses a grounded scene got wrong. Hanzo-measured; the sealed set is private.
Finding the right tool in a large catalog

Kai’s tool-relevance head, in development, ranks a shortlist of 32 tools drawn from the whole catalog. The shortlist is an open embedding model, zen-embedding-0.6B, with a small BM25 term; nothing is trained for it. Here it is scored against BM25 alone on a dev catalog Hanzo assembled from public tool-calling sets and its own API: 2,928 tools, 6,608 requests.

Claude Code Acceleration: Zero-Model Fault Repair (Kai)
Claude Code Acceleration: Atomic AST Refactoring
In-process Trigram + Tree-Sitter AST context bundle (0 daemons)
Zero Docker, Zero background model daemons
Qdrant Vector DB container + Ollama mxbai-embed-large (10 GB)
Claude Code / Cursor (Raw Grep + File Reads)
Iterative grep + full file reads over stdio (8 roundtrips to LLM)

In a real agentic workflow (e.g. Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf), each tool roundtrip incurs an additional 3–5 seconds of LLM inference latency. By replacing 6–13 iterative file exploration roundtrips with Hanzo’s in-process AST indexing (`code_context`, `code_tool`, `hanzo_refactor`) and Kai deterministic test-driven search, Hanzo Dev accelerates Claude Code by
20× to 50× (and up to 137× on zero-model search-settled faults)

Heap per live agent, a goroutine

A live agent here is a goroutine: it shares one address space with every other, and nothing about it is an isolation boundary. Code that has to be isolated gets a microVM. The goroutine timings are the median of one pass on an Apple M4 Max, 16 cores. Every figure here is transcribed from the harness's README rather than read from a run file, and each page names the command that prints it.

Each build pulls the latest validated runs from the research API: canonical, public, and not flagged inconsistent. When the API cannot be read, or answers with fewer runs than the committed snapshot already holds, the build keeps the snapshot, and the page swaps in what the API holds once it answers in the browser.
A run is dated by when it ended; the platform bench records its month.

Live is the newest run the API serves for a benchmark. Frozen is a committed run file, a snapshot, or a figure transcribed from a harness’s README. Superseded is an earlier run of the same benchmark that a later one replaced; it stays in the library, so a revision’s history can be read.
Kai’s and Enso’s rows are research runs, served at

and read when this page opens. The memory, graph and code panels read the committed run files of the benchmarks repository. Kai’s yes/no table and the tool shortlist are Hanzo-measured reads the research API does not file: each is its run’s report, copied unchanged, and names its model, date and count.
Every frontier point is a run Hanzo filed: the router and each single model on the same questions, at the same tag. No vendor-reported figure is on a board here.

Kai beside Jev is the input-token rate each is billed, from the price list, not a cost per task. The frontier’s axis is what each run spent on the whole question set. No speed is claimed here without a measured comparison; latency, where this Kai version was timed, is in its tables.

A frontier is drawn among the rows of one benchmark, never across two, and a leaderboard row compares two models on one suite. Suites measure different tasks, so the mean is a summary, not a score on any of them.
